title: MANDEL: Manslaughter charges dropped for three cops in child's shooting death
article: That poor baby was sitting in his father's lap.

In an Oshawa courtroom, prosecutors revealed that startling fact as they withdrew all charges against three OPP officers in the 2020 accidental shooting of a 19-month-old toddler kidnapped by his troubled gun-wielding father.
Jameson Shapiro died at the scene in Kawartha Lakes. His dad, William Shapiro, 33, succumbed to his injuries about a week later.

"While the evidence establishes that Jameson Shapiro died as the result of at least one police\-fired bullet, the Crown has concluded that, for the purposes of this criminal prosecution, his death was the tragic, unintended consequence of shots fired by the defendants in a genuine situation of self-defence," prosecutor Ian Bulmer told Justice Paul Bellefontaine.
After recently receiving the officers' notes, he and fellow Crown attorney Peter Scrutton concluded the trio had reasonable reason to believe Shapiro might turn his stolen Colt 45 on police.
"It is clear that William Shapiro is the person who was most responsible for the events that occurred that day," he said.

Kawartha Lake OPP constables Nathan Vanderheyden, Kenneth Pengelly and Grayson Cappus were charged by the Special Investigations Unit with manslaughter, aggravated assault and reckless discharge of a firearm in the November 2020 tragedy.
Relatives and colleagues in the courtroom embraced Pengelly and Cappus. Vanderheyden had appeared by video.
Also in court was Const. Chris Dobbs, who also almost died that day after the fleeing William rammed his Toyota Tundra pickup into his police cruiser.
"What happened on Nov. 26, 2020 was a terrible, dangerous and traumatic event for everyone involved," Bulmer said.

With a criminal record for domestic violence, documented mental health issues and a fixation on deficiencies in his Trent Lakes home, Shapiro had appeared in his estranged wife's bedroom about 3 a.m. He told Tara Shapiro he was going to "kill all of them," the "real estate agents" and himself, according to an agreed statement of fact. He then abducted Jameson, taking him into his pickup that had no baby car seat.

After the OPP were notified, Vanderheyden reported to dispatch that he could see William driving his rusty truck at high speed and had pointed a handgun at his own head. Officers on the radio reported he had mental health issues and had been suicidal.
Vanderheyden sought confirmation on whether the abducted toddler was in the vehicle and whether he should end his pursuit.
The OPP dispatcher confirmed the baby was in the truck, but Bulmer said that information "may not have been heard by everyone who responded to the call."

At about 9 a.m., the Crown said, police decided to end the chase by placing spike belts across Pigeon Lake Rd. Dobbs had placed his across the westbound lane when Shapiro, travelling at 171 km/h just four seconds before impact, swerved right at the last moment and slammed into Dobbs' cruiser as he crouched in front.
Dobbs' "catastrophic" injuries included a broken neck, back and two fractured legs
Bulmer said all the evidence indicated the officers had acted "reasonably and diligently" up to that point, but there was a "gap" in the narrative: what did they see that caused them to open fire?

Investigators examine the scene on County Road 17 in Kawartha Lakes, Ont., after a deadly police shooting that killed toddler Jameson Shapiro and his gun-wielding father, on Nov. 26, 2020. (Photo by Fred Thornhill, The Canadian Press)
Their lawyers recently agreed to disclose the notes officers made after the deadly shooting to explain for the first time why they'd resorted to force - and that changed everything.
After the crash, Vanderheyden said he could see movement behind William's deployed airbag and repeatedly demanded he drop his weapon. Instead, he responded with "F- you."

Vanderheyden aimed his rifle and fired a first burst of rounds downward into the driver's seat, and again yelled for him to drop his gun and show his hands. He then saw William's arm emerge from the airbag curtain holding a handgun that swung in his direction. He immediately fired again; Pengally and Cappus said they also believed officer safety was at risk and fired as well.
Vanderheyden fired 25 times from his Colt C-8 semiautomatic rifle, Pengally fired his rifle three times, while Cappus fired his Glock handgun 17 times.

A forensic analysis of William's stolen gun, found on the driver's side floor, showed there was an unfired cartridge stuck in the ejection port and another in the breach of the barrel, suggesting it may have jammed.

"The Crown does not have a basis upon which to challenge or contradict the recently disclosed officers' accounts that they believed William Shapiro was about to apply deadly force, a threat to which they were legally entitled to respond with deadly force," the prosecutor explained.
That poor child survived the collision but suffered four gunshot wounds, the fatal one entering the base of his skull.

"The blood stain pattern analysis as well as DNA samples of the blood in the Tundra establish that both William and Jameson Shapiro occupied the driver's seat of the Tundra at the time they suffered their gunshot wounds," Bulmer said.

"No evidence suggests that (police) ought to have anticipated his presence in his father's lap at the time of the shooting, and it is not unreasonable to have assumed he was positioned elsewhere in the Tundra at the time the shots were fired."
Of course, they couldn't have known - but was deploying two high-powered rifles at such close proximity the best choice?
Their lawyers said the OPP officers have endured more than three years of hell as they've carried the horror of that painful day as well as the weight of their legal jeopardy.
"It's the just and right outcome," said lawyer Joseph Markson, as Pengelly, a 48-year police veteran, stood behind him.

"The circumstances of this incident involving the death of an innocent child are tragic for all involved," said OPP Association President John Cerasuolo in a statement. "Unfortunately, as police officers protect public safety in highly volatile and fast-moving dangerous situations, unexpected outcomes may result."
But that shouldn't be the end of this horrific story - there must be an inquest to address so many questions that remain.
